newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Black S.Africans slam Malan acquittal as unjust.
newsitem.headline: Black S.Africans slam Malan acquittal as unjust.

text.p: Black South Africans lamented Friday's acquittal of ex-defence minister Magnus Malan and other apartheid chiefs on murder charges, saying President Nelson Mandela had yet to persuade them true justice reigned.

"The outcome of this case shows everyone high up can do as he pleases. Perpetrators of evil are still going to reign high here because nothing has changed," said a 50-year-old Zulu man, leaning against court railings in the hope of glimpsing Malan.

Malan, the highest apartheid-era figure to be tried for atrocities to preserve white rule, was cleared of masterminding a plan that led to a 1987 attack near Durban in which 13 black children and adults died.

"There is just no justice in this country. There is no difference between this case and a kangaroo court where only one side is favoured... and the killers are set free," said 60-year-old Louise, visibly upset.
"I am very upset. What is the government afraid of, is it fear for an Afrikaner backlash? These people did not commit suicide," she added.
Ordinary white South Africans seemed indifferent to the judgment. Most who were asked for comment said they had paid scant attention to the trial heard in Durban.
"The process of justice had to be seen getting done. I am not interested in politics. This was all politics," said one white businessman.

Mandela's African National Congress and human rights activists have often accused South Africa's mostly white judges of meting out racially biased justice and want an overhaul of the entire judicial system.
Also bewildered by Judge Jan Hugo's decision was Mbusi Ntuli, 23, a brother of the ANC sympathiser who was the intended target in the 1987 attack.
Ntuli, whose brother was not at home when the massacre was carried out, said "the government has proven to be afraid to take the bull by its horns".
"I am losing confidence that this new government will ever find truth about what happened," he told reporters.
Mandela reiterated his government's commitment to justice and truth, saying, "We will continue to investigate who was responsible."
"The Bible says we must forgive, may be some people will forgive Malan, but I don't know if it is possible in this case."
